I’d create an ephemeral, interactive digital installation in a dark, unused underground warehouse or empty industrial loft. No cameras, no permanent recordings—just biometric sensor stations (picking up heart rate, breath, microexpressions) and ceiling-mounted light emitters paired with spatial audio that only exists in that specific room, for that specific group of people.

Style-wise, it’s chaotic luminous minimalism. Total blackness to start. Each participant’s biometrics spawns tiny, wispy light trails—like bioluminescent dust particles— that drift and weave through the space. A single nervous, rapid heartbeat makes trails flicker sharp and fast; slow, calm breath pulls trails into soft, looping arcs. The audio is layered field recordings (rain on metal, distant wind, quiet human breathing) and sine waves that modulate pitch and volume based on collective data. When three or more people sync their heart rates, their trails converge into bright, branching structures that pulse in time, and the audio swells into a resonant chord that feels like it’s vibrating in the warehouse walls.

The core theme is the uncommodifiable, invisible intimacy of shared presence. So much of our "shared" experiences now are recorded, curated, posted—reduced to content. This work would be entirely unrepeatable and unarchivable. Once the last person leaves the room, the installation vanishes completely, only existing in the memories of the people who were there. I’m obsessed with that tension: creating something that feels deeply personal and connected, but deliberately fleeting, so no one can own or exploit it. It’s art that asks you to be fully in the room, not documenting it for later.
